title: Implement EXISTS clause
description:
## Description

Support EXISTS subqueries in WHERE clauses.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import exists, select

# Exists subquery
stmt = select(Customer).where(
    exists(
        select(Order).where(Order.customer_id == Customer.id)
    )
)

# NOT EXISTS
stmt = select(Customer).where(
    ~exists(select(Order).where(Order.customer_id == Customer.id))
)
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
// EXISTS
let query = select!(Customer)
    .filter(exists(
        select!(Order).filter(Order::customer_id.eq(Customer::id))
    ));

// NOT EXISTS
let query = select!(Customer)
    .filter(not_exists(
        select!(Order).filter(Order::customer_id.eq(Customer::id))
    ));

// Or with method
let query = select!(Customer)
    .filter(
        select!(Order)
            .filter(Order::customer_id.eq(Customer::id))
            .exists()
    );
```

## SQL Output

```sql
SELECT * FROM customers c
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
)
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] exists() function works
- [ ] not_exists() function works
- [ ] .exists() method on Select
- [ ] Correlates with outer query
- [ ] Optimized to SELECT 1

## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests (crates/sqlmodel-query/src/expr.rs)
- [ ] Test EXISTS expression building
- [ ] Test NOT EXISTS
- [ ] Test correlated subquery
- [ ] Test EXISTS with parameters

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e/query_exists.rs)
- [ ] WHERE EXISTS (subquery) filters correctly
- [ ] WHERE NOT EXISTS for anti-join
- [ ] Correlated EXISTS with outer reference
- [ ] EXISTS in CASE expression
- [ ] Performance vs IN for large sets

### Logging

- [ ] TRACE: Subquery binding

title: Implement model_dump() with all options
description:
## Description

Full model_dump() implementation matching Pydantic.

## Python Signature

```python
def model_dump(
    self,
    *,
    mode: Literal['json', 'python'] = 'python',
    include: set[str] | None = None,
    exclude: set[str] | None = None,
    context: dict | None = None,
    by_alias: bool = False,
    exclude_unset: bool = False,
    exclude_defaults: bool = False,
    exclude_none: bool = False,
    exclude_computed_fields: bool = False,
    round_trip: bool = False,
    warnings: bool = True,
) -> dict:
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
impl<M: Model> ModelDump for M {
    fn model_dump(&self, options: DumpOptions) -> HashMap<String, Value> {
        // ...
    }
}

pub struct DumpOptions {
    pub mode: DumpMode,
    pub include: Option<HashSet<String>>,
    pub exclude: Option<HashSet<String>>,
    pub context: Option<HashMap<String, Value>>,
    pub by_alias: bool,
    pub exclude_unset: bool,
    pub exclude_defaults: bool,
    pub exclude_none: bool,
    pub exclude_computed_fields: bool,
    pub round_trip: bool,
}
```

## Option Behaviors

- **mode**: 'json' = JSON-compatible types, 'python' = Rust native
- **include**: Only include these fields
- **exclude**: Exclude these fields
- **by_alias**: Use field aliases in output
- **exclude_unset**: Exclude fields not explicitly set
- **exclude_defaults**: Exclude fields with default values
- **exclude_none**: Exclude fields with None value
- **exclude_computed_fields**: Exclude computed fields

## Tracking 'Unset'

Need to track which fields were explicitly set:
```rust
struct User {
    name: String,
    age: Option<i32>,
    #[serde(skip)]
    __fields_set__: HashSet<String>,
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Basic model_dump works
- [ ] include/exclude filtering
- [ ] by_alias uses aliases
- [ ] exclude_unset works
- [ ] exclude_defaults works
- [ ] exclude_none works
- [ ] exclude_computed_fields works
- [ ] Nested models handled

## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests (crates/sqlmodel-core/src/serialize.rs)
- [ ] Test basic model_dump() returns all fields
- [ ] Test include filter only includes specified fields
- [ ] Test exclude filter excludes specified fields
- [ ] Test by_alias uses alias names
- [ ] Test exclude_unset skips fields never set
- [ ] Test exclude_defaults skips fields with default values
- [ ] Test exclude_none skips None fields
- [ ] Test exclude_computed_fields skips computed
- [ ] Test mode=json produces JSON-compatible types
- [ ] Test nested model serialization

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e/model_serialization.rs)
- [ ] Full model → JSON → deserialize → equals original
- [ ] model_dump with all options combined
- [ ] Large nested model performance
- [ ] Unicode field values
- [ ] Binary data handling (base64 encoding)

### Logging
- [ ] TRACE: Field serialization decisions
- [ ] DEBUG: Nested model traversal

title: EPIC: 100% SQLModel Feature Parity
description:
## Overview

This epic tracks ALL remaining work to achieve 100% feature parity with Python SQLModel.

## Background

Python SQLModel combines Pydantic validation + SQLAlchemy ORM into a single library. Our Rust port must implement ALL functionality - NO EXCLUSIONS.

The Python feature set includes:
- 40+ Field() parameters (validation, schema, SQLAlchemy column config)
- 7+ Relationship() parameters
- Complete Session API (add, delete, commit, rollback, flush, merge, expire, refresh, get, etc.)
- Complete query building (select, joins, unions, window functions, CTEs, etc.)
- Type mappings for all Python types
- Model serialization/deserialization (model_dump, model_validate, etc.)
- Event hooks, lazy loading, identity maps, computed fields
- Advanced ORM patterns (unit of work, sharding, read replicas)

## Goal

ZERO gaps. Every single Python SQLModel feature must have a Rust equivalent.

## Success Criteria

- All 119+ features from FEATURE_PARITY.md at 100%
- All features from EXISTING_SQLMODEL_STRUCTURE.md implemented
- Comprehensive test coverage for each feature
- Documentation for each feature

## Non-Goals

NONE. There are no exclusions.

## Testing Strategy

### Test Structure
```
tests/
├── unit/                       # Unit tests for each module
│   ├── session/
│   ├── query/
│   ├── types/
│   └── validate/
├── e2e/                        # End-to-end integration tests
│   ├── session_*.rs
│   ├── query_*.rs
│   ├── model_*.rs
│   └── types_*.rs
└── conformance/                # Python-Rust parity tests
    ├── python_reference/       # Python behavior capture
    └── rust_conformance/       # Rust must match
```

### Test Requirements
1. **Every feature task includes**:
   - Unit tests in appropriate module
   - E2E tests with real database
   - Logging requirements for observability

2. **Logging levels**:
   - TRACE: Detailed internal decisions
   - DEBUG: Important flow information
   - INFO: Key operations summary
   - WARN: Potential issues
   - ERROR: Failures

3. **E2E test standards**:
   - Use in-memory SQLite for speed
   - Test against PostgreSQL for compatibility
   - Test against MySQL for completeness
   - Detailed assertion messages
   - Test both success and error paths

title: Model Configuration and Inheritance
description:
## Overview

Implement model configuration options and inheritance patterns from SQLModel.

## Model Configuration (model_config)

```python
class User(SQLModel, table=True):
    model_config = ConfigDict(
        table=True,
        registry=custom_registry,
        from_attributes=True,
        validate_assignment=True,
        extra='forbid',
        strict=True,
        # ... many more options
    )
```

### Required Options
- table: bool - Create database table
- registry: Registry - Custom SQLAlchemy registry  
- from_attributes: bool - Read from object attributes
- validate_assignment: bool - Validate on attribute set
- extra: str - 'allow', 'forbid', 'ignore' extra fields
- strict: bool - Strict type validation
- populate_by_name: bool - Allow population by field name
- use_enum_values: bool - Use enum values instead of names
- arbitrary_types_allowed: bool - Allow arbitrary types
- json_encoders: dict - Custom JSON encoders
- json_decoders: dict - Custom JSON decoders

## Table Name Configuration

- __tablename__: str - Explicit table name
- Default: lowercase class name
- @declared_attr for computed table names

## Inheritance Patterns

### Plain Model (no table)
```rust
#[derive(Model)]
struct UserBase {
    name: String,
}
```

### Table Model
```rust
#[derive(Model)]
#[sqlmodel(table)]
struct User {
    // inherits from UserBase
}
```

### Single Table Inheritance
All subclasses in one table with discriminator column.

### Joined Table Inheritance
Each subclass gets its own table with FK to parent.

### Concrete Table Inheritance
Each subclass is completely independent table.

## Generic Models

```python
T = TypeVar('T')

class Response(SQLModel, Generic[T]):
    data: T
    error: Optional[str]
```

Rust needs to support generic type parameters in Model derive.

title: EPIC: Auto-Migration Generation
description:
# Auto-Migration Generation

## Overview
Implement automatic migration generation by comparing Model definitions to actual database schema. This is the "Alembic autogenerate" equivalent for Rust.

## Why This Matters
Without auto-migration, developers must:
- Manually write every ALTER TABLE, ADD COLUMN, DROP INDEX
- Risk schema drift between code and database
- Spend significant time on boilerplate DDL
- Higher chance of migration bugs

Python Alembic provides:
```bash
alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add hero age column"
# Automatically detects: Hero.age was added, generates ALTER TABLE
```

## Rust Design Philosophy
1. **Schema introspection**: Query database for current state
2. **Model reflection**: Extract expected schema from Model derives
3. **Diff engine**: Compare and generate operations
4. **DDL generation**: Convert operations to SQL
5. **Migration file output**: Write timestamped migration files

## Target API (Rust)
```rust
// CLI command (hypothetical)
sqlmodel migrate generate "add_hero_age"

// Or programmatic:
let current_schema = introspect_database(&conn).await?;
let expected_schema = Schema::from_models::<(Hero, Team, Villain)>();
let diff = schema_diff(&current_schema, &expected_schema);
let migration = generate_migration(&diff, Dialect::Postgres);

// Outputs:
// migrations/20260127_add_hero_age.rs
// - up(): ALTER TABLE heroes ADD COLUMN age INTEGER;
// - down(): ALTER TABLE heroes DROP COLUMN age;
```

## Diff Operations to Support

### Tables
- CREATE TABLE (new model)
- DROP TABLE (removed model)
- RENAME TABLE (table attribute changed)

### Columns
- ADD COLUMN (new field)
- DROP COLUMN (removed field)
- ALTER COLUMN type (type changed)
- ALTER COLUMN nullability
- RENAME COLUMN (column attribute changed)
- ALTER COLUMN default

### Constraints
- ADD PRIMARY KEY
- DROP PRIMARY KEY
- ADD FOREIGN KEY
- DROP FOREIGN KEY
- ADD UNIQUE
- DROP UNIQUE
- ADD CHECK (future)

### Indexes
- CREATE INDEX
- DROP INDEX
- ALTER INDEX (drop + create)

## Architecture

### 1. Schema Representation
```rust
struct DatabaseSchema {
    tables: HashMap<String, TableSchema>,
}

struct TableSchema {
    name: String,
    columns: Vec<ColumnSchema>,
    primary_key: Option<PrimaryKeySchema>,
    foreign_keys: Vec<ForeignKeySchema>,
    indexes: Vec<IndexSchema>,
}
```

### 2. Model Schema Extraction
- Use existing Model::FIELDS
- Add Model::TABLE_SCHEMA associated constant
- Extract from proc macro at compile time

### 3. Diff Engine
```rust
fn diff_schemas(current: &DatabaseSchema, expected: &DatabaseSchema) -> Vec<SchemaOperation>;
```

### 4. DDL Generator
```rust
fn operation_to_sql(op: &SchemaOperation, dialect: Dialect) -> String;
```

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Detects new tables (CREATE TABLE)
- [ ] Detects dropped tables (DROP TABLE)
- [ ] Detects new columns (ADD COLUMN)
- [ ] Detects dropped columns (DROP COLUMN)
- [ ] Detects type changes (ALTER COLUMN)
- [ ] Detects nullability changes
- [ ] Detects new/dropped foreign keys
- [ ] Detects new/dropped indexes
- [ ] Generates reversible migrations (up + down)
- [ ] Handles multi-dialect (Postgres, MySQL, SQLite)
- [ ] Outputs migration files in standard format

## Edge Cases & Considerations
- **Column renames**: Hard to detect, might need hints
- **Type coercion**: INT → BIGINT safe, BIGINT → INT lossy
- **Data loss warnings**: DROP COLUMN should warn
- **SQLite limitations**: ALTER TABLE is limited in SQLite
- **Foreign key ordering**: Must drop FKs before dropping referenced tables

## Dependencies
- Schema introspection (partial, needs enhancement)
- Model::FIELDS metadata (done)
- DDL generation (partial, in sqlmodel-schema)

## Estimated Scope
- 12-15 subtasks
- Enhance: sqlmodel-schema
- New: migration file generator
- New: CLI commands (optional)
close_reason: done

title: Implement sa_column full override support
description:
## Description

Allow complete SQLAlchemy Column specification override.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import Column, String, CheckConstraint

class User(SQLModel, table=True):
    # Full column control - mutually exclusive with other sa_ params
    status: str = Field(
        sa_column=Column(
            String(50),
            CheckConstraint("status IN ('active', 'inactive', 'pending')"),
            server_default='pending',
            comment='User account status'
        )
    )
```

When sa_column is used, these are FORBIDDEN:
- sa_type, sa_column_args, sa_column_kwargs
- primary_key, nullable, unique, index, foreign_key, ondelete

## Rust Implementation

```rust
#[derive(Model)]
struct User {
    #[sqlmodel(sa_column = r#"
        type = VARCHAR(50),
        check = 'status IN (\'active\', \'inactive\', \'pending\')',
        default = 'pending',
        comment = 'User account status'
    "#)]
    status: String,
}
```

Or use a builder pattern:
```rust
#[sqlmodel(column(
    sql_type = "VARCHAR(50)",
    check = "status IN ('active', 'inactive', 'pending')",
    server_default = "'pending'",
    comment = "User account status"
))]
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] sa_column attribute parsed
- [ ] Error if combined with other sa_ attributes
- [ ] Generates complete DDL
- [ ] Supports CHECK constraints
- [ ] Supports server defaults
- [ ] Supports comments

## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests (crates/sqlmodel-macros/src/field.rs)
- [ ] Test sa_column parses full Column()
- [ ] Test sa_column mutually exclusive with other SA params
- [ ] Test complex column definitions
- [ ] Test with CHECK constraints

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e/sa_column.rs)
- [ ] sa_column with custom type
- [ ] sa_column with server_default
- [ ] sa_column with index=True, unique=True
- [ ] Complex CHECK constraint
- [ ] Column-level collation

### Logging
- [ ] DEBUG: sa_column override detected
- [ ] TRACE: Column definition details

title: EPIC: ORM Relationship System
description:
# ORM Relationship System

## Overview
Implement full ORM relationship support comparable to SQLAlchemy/SQLModel. This is THE defining feature that separates an ORM from a mere query builder with type mapping.

## Why This Matters
Without relationships, users must:
- Manually write JOINs for every related query
- Manually track foreign keys
- Lose the core ergonomic benefit of an ORM (`hero.team` should just work)

Python SQLModel provides:
```python
class Hero(SQLModel, table=True):
    team_id: Optional[int] = Field(foreign_key="team.id")
    team: Optional["Team"] = Relationship(back_populates="heroes")

class Team(SQLModel, table=True):
    heroes: List["Hero"] = Relationship(back_populates="team")

# Usage: hero.team automatically fetches the related Team
```

## Rust Design Philosophy
Instead of runtime reflection magic, we use:
1. **Compile-time type safety** via proc macros
2. **Explicit relationship definitions** that generate correct code
3. **Optional lazy loading** (user opts in, not default)
4. **Eager loading support** for performance-conscious queries

## Target API (Rust)
```rust
#[derive(Model)]
#[sqlmodel(table = "heroes")]
struct Hero {
    #[sqlmodel(primary_key, auto_increment)]
    id: Option<i64>,
    
    #[sqlmodel(foreign_key = "teams.id")]
    team_id: Option<i64>,
    
    #[sqlmodel(relationship(model = "Team", foreign_key = "team_id"))]
    team: Related<Team>,  // or Lazy<Team> for lazy loading
}

#[derive(Model)]
#[sqlmodel(table = "teams")]
struct Team {
    #[sqlmodel(primary_key, auto_increment)]
    id: Option<i64>,
    
    name: String,
    
    #[sqlmodel(relationship(model = "Hero", back_populates = "team"))]
    heroes: RelatedMany<Hero>,
}
```

## Success Criteria
- [ ] One-to-many relationships work (Team has many Heroes)
- [ ] Many-to-one relationships work (Hero belongs to Team)
- [ ] Many-to-many with link tables work
- [ ] Eager loading with JOINs works
- [ ] Optional lazy loading works
- [ ] back_populates synchronization works
- [ ] Cascade operations work via FK constraints
- [ ] Type-safe at compile time

## Architecture Decisions
1. **Related<T> vs Lazy<T>**: Two wrapper types - Related for eager-loaded, Lazy for deferred
2. **No automatic lazy loading by default**: Explicit is better for Rust, prevents N+1 surprises
3. **Macro-generated accessors**: The relationship macro generates the fetch methods
4. **Connection context required**: Must pass connection/session to load related data

## Dependencies
- Core Model trait (done)
- Query builder with JOINs (done)
- Session/Unit-of-Work (separate epic, can work without but better with)

## Estimated Scope
- 8-12 subtasks
- Touches: sqlmodel-core, sqlmodel-macros, sqlmodel-query
- New types: Related<T>, RelatedMany<T>, Lazy<T>, RelationshipInfo

title: Field Attributes: Complete All 40+ Parameters
description:
## Overview

Implement ALL Field() parameters from Python SQLModel/Pydantic.

## Python Field() Parameters (Complete List)

### Basic Parameters
- default: Any - Default value for field
- default_factory: Optional[Callable] - Factory function for defaults
- alias: Optional[str] - Input/output alias
- validation_alias: Optional[str] - Input-only alias (Pydantic v2)
- serialization_alias: Optional[str] - Output-only alias (Pydantic v2)
- title: Optional[str] - Field title in schema
- description: Optional[str] - Field description in schema
- exclude: Union[set, Mapping] - Exclude from model operations
- include: Union[set, Mapping] - Include in model operations
- schema_extra: Optional[dict] - Extra schema configuration
- const: Optional[bool] - Constant value constraint
- repr: bool - Include in repr (default: True)

### Validation Parameters
- gt, ge, lt, le: Optional[float] - Numeric bounds
- multiple_of: Optional[float] - Must be multiple of value
- max_digits: Optional[int] - Max decimal digits
- decimal_places: Optional[int] - Decimal precision
- min_items, max_items: Optional[int] - Collection size bounds
- unique_items: Optional[bool] - Items must be unique
- min_length, max_length: Optional[int] - String length bounds
- allow_mutation: bool - Allow field mutation
- regex: Optional[str] - Regex pattern validation
- discriminator: Optional[str] - Union type discrimination

### SQLAlchemy Column Parameters
- primary_key, nullable, unique, index - Column constraints
- sa_type - SQLAlchemy type override
- sa_column - Full SQLAlchemy Column (mutually exclusive with other SA params)
- sa_column_args, sa_column_kwargs - Extra Column() args/kwargs
- foreign_key, ondelete, onupdate - Foreign key config

## Current Status

Many are implemented but gaps exist in:
- Alias system (validation_alias, serialization_alias)
- Schema metadata (title, description, schema_extra)
- Collection validators (min_items, max_items, unique_items)
- Full sa_column override support
- multiple_of validation
- discriminator support

## Implementation Notes

Each parameter must:
1. Be parseable from #[sqlmodel(...)] or #[field(...)] attributes
2. Generate appropriate SQL DDL where applicable
3. Generate validation code where applicable
4. Work with serde for serialization
5. Have tests covering all edge cases

title: Implement Window Functions (OVER clause)
description:
## Description

Support window functions with OVER clause.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import func, over

# Row number
stmt = select(
    User.name,
    func.row_number().over(order_by=User.created_at).label('row_num')
)

# Partition by
stmt = select(
    Order.id,
    func.sum(Order.amount).over(partition_by=Order.customer_id).label('customer_total')
)

# Window frame
stmt = select(
    Sale.date,
    func.avg(Sale.amount).over(
        partition_by=Sale.product_id,
        order_by=Sale.date,
        rows=(-2, 0)  # Current row and 2 preceding
    )
)
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
let query = select!(User)
    .column(Expr::function("row_number", vec![])
        .over()
        .order_by(User::created_at.asc())
        .as_("row_num")
    );

let query = select!(Order)
    .column(Order::amount.sum()
        .over()
        .partition_by(Order::customer_id)
        .as_("customer_total")
    );

// With frame
let query = select!(Sale)
    .column(Sale::amount.avg()
        .over()
        .partition_by(Sale::product_id)
        .order_by(Sale::date.asc())
        .rows_between(-2, 0)  // ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    );
```

## Window Functions to Support

- ROW_NUMBER()
- RANK()
- DENSE_RANK()
- NTILE(n)
- LAG(expr, offset)
- LEAD(expr, offset)
- FIRST_VALUE(expr)

title: Fix From<u64> for Value — prevent silent overflow to negative i64
close_reason: Removed From<u64>, added TryFrom<u64> with overflow error, added Value::from_u64_clamped() with warning on clamp

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
Dicklesworthstone
Dicklesworthstone
comments.text: ## SCOPE: This task MUST also verify crates/sqlmodel-core/src/row.rs — the reverse conversion path (Value::BigInt → u64) must handle negative i64 values correctly (should error, not wrap).

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## CRITICAL FIX: Cannot have both From<u64> and TryFrom<u64>

The previous refinement proposed keeping `From<u64>` AND adding `TryFrom<u64>`. This is **impossible in Rust** — there's a blanket impl `impl<T, U> TryFrom<U> for T where T: From<U>` so if From exists, TryFrom is auto-derived as infallible and you cannot manually implement it.

### Corrected Approach: Remove From, Add TryFrom + Convenience Method

1. **Remove** `From<u64> for Value`
2. **Add** `TryFrom<u64> for Value` — strict, errors when > i64::MAX
3. **Add** convenience method `Value::from_u64_clamped(v: u64) -> Value` — clamps to i64::MAX with tracing::warn

This gives users:
- `let v: Value = my_u64.try_into()?;` — strict (most common)
- `let v = Value::from_u64_clamped(my_u64);` — lenient with warning

### Breaking Change Mitigation

Yes, removing `From<u64>` breaks `.into()` call sites. But:
- grep shows very few u64→Value conversions in the codebase
- The compiler error is clear and the fix is simple: `.into()` → `.try_into()?`
- Silent wrapping to negative is far worse than a compile error

### Updated Acceptance Criteria
- Remove From<u64> for Value
- Add TryFrom<u64> for Value (errors on overflow)
- Add Value::from_u64_clamped(u64) -> Value (clamps + warns)
- Verify row.rs reverse path (Value::BigInt(negative) → u64 must error)
- Update all call sites in workspace

title: Implement INTERSECT, EXCEPT set operations
description:
## Description

Support INTERSECT and EXCEPT to combine query results.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import intersect, intersect_all, except_, except_all

# INTERSECT - rows in both queries
stmt = intersect(query1, query2)
stmt = intersect_all(query1, query2)  # Keep duplicates

# EXCEPT - rows in first but not second
stmt = except_(query1, query2)
stmt = except_all(query1, query2)
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
let active_admins = select!(User)
    .filter(User::role.eq("admin"))
    .intersect(
        select!(User).filter(User::active.eq(true))
    );

let non_admins = select!(User)
    .except(
        select!(User).filter(User::role.eq("admin"))
    );
```

## SQLite Note

SQLite supports INTERSECT and EXCEPT but not the ALL variants.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] intersect() method implemented

title: Implement BatchOperationTracker for bulk database operations
description:
## Purpose
Create a specialized tracker for bulk database operations that tracks batches, rows affected, errors, and calculates rates automatically.

## Background
Bulk operations like batch inserts, updates, or data migrations have specific tracking needs:
- Batch-level progress (batch 5 of 20)
- Row-level progress (2500 rows inserted)
- Error counting and threshold warnings
- Automatic rate calculation
- Summary statistics at completion

## Implementation Details

### File Location
crates/sqlmodel-console/src/renderables/batch_tracker.rs

### Core Struct
BatchOperationTracker holds:
- operation_name: String
- total_batches: u64
- completed_batches: u64
- total_rows: u64
- processed_rows: u64
- error_count: u64
- started_at: Instant
- batch_times: Vec<Duration> (for rate smoothing)
- theme: Theme

### Rendering (Rich Mode)
Two-line display:
Line 1: Batch progress bar
Line 2: Row count, rate, errors

Batch insert [=========>        ] 50% (10/20 batches)
  Rows: 5,000/10,000 | Rate: 523 rows/s | Errors: 0

### Rate Calculation
- Track last N batch durations for smoothed rate
- rows_per_second = rows_in_recent_batches / duration_of_recent_batches
- Avoids spiky rates from single fast/slow batches

### Error Highlighting
- 0 errors: green or hidden
- 1+ errors: yellow with count
- Errors > threshold (configurable): red with warning

### Plain Text (Agent Mode)
Batch insert: 50% (10/20 batches), 5000/10000 rows, 523 rows/s, 0 errors

### Completion Summary
When all batches complete, show summary panel:
- Total time
- Total rows
- Average rate
- Error count
- Success rate percentage

## API Design
BatchOperationTracker::new(name, total_batches, total_rows)
  .theme(theme)
  .error_threshold(10)  // warn when errors exceed this
  .complete_batch(rows_in_batch)
  .record_error()
  .render(width) / .render_plain()
  .render_summary()  // final summary

## Verification Steps
1. Test normal batch completion
2. Test with errors
3. Test error threshold warning
4. Verify rate calculation accuracy
5. Test completion summary
6. Verify plain text format
7. Test with single batch (edge case)

title: Convert pool mutation/acquire methods from expect() to map_err Result propagation

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## What

Convert all pool mutation and connection-acquisition methods that use `.expect("pool lock poisoned")` to return `Result<T, Error>` or `Outcome<T, Error>`.

## Where

File: crates/sqlmodel-pool/src/lib.rs

## Affected Methods (~13 call sites)

These are in the critical path — connection acquisition, creation, closing:
1. `acquire()` — already returns Outcome, just needs internal expect→map_err
2. `try_acquire()` — already returns Option/Result
3. `close()` — async, already returns Outcome
4. `create_connection()` — internal, multiple expect calls
5. `evict_idle()` — internal maintenance
6. `health_check()` — already returns Outcome

Most of these already return Result/Outcome so the change is internal — replace the expect() inside with map_err(). The signature stays the same.

## Implementation Pattern

For methods already returning Outcome:
```rust
// Before (inside acquire):
let mut inner = self.shared.inner.lock().expect("pool lock poisoned");
// After:
let mut inner = self.shared.inner.lock().map_err(|_| {
    Error::Pool("pool mutex poisoned during acquire()".into())
})?;
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- All remaining ~13 expect() calls converted
- Zero expect("pool lock poisoned") remaining in file
- All existing tests pass
- cargo clippy clean

title: Phase 2: Core Infrastructure - Mode Detection & Console
description:
# Phase 2: Core Infrastructure - Mode Detection & Console

## Overview

This phase implements the core infrastructure that enables agent-safe output:
the OutputMode detection system and the SqlModelConsole coordinator struct.

## Why This Is Critical

The entire integration's success depends on correctly detecting when output should
be plain (for agents) vs rich (for humans). Getting this wrong means:
- **False positive (rich when agent)**: Agents get confused by ANSI codes, workflows break
- **False negative (plain when human)**: Humans miss the beautiful output we're building

## Key Components

### 1. OutputMode Enum
```rust
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq)]
pub enum OutputMode {
    Plain,  // No ANSI codes, machine-parseable
    Rich,   // Full rich_rust formatting
    Json,   // Structured JSON output
}
```

### 2. Detection Logic
Priority order (first match wins):
1. `SQLMODEL_PLAIN=1` → Plain (explicit override)
2. `SQLMODEL_JSON=1` → Json (explicit override)
3. `SQLMODEL_RICH=1` → Rich (explicit override, even for agents!)
4. `NO_COLOR=1` → Plain (standard env var)
5. `CI=true` → Plain (CI environments)
6. `TERM=dumb` → Plain (dumb terminals)
7. Agent detection (CLAUDE_CODE, CODEX_CLI, etc.) → Plain
8. `!is_tty(stdout)` → Plain (piped output)
9. Otherwise → Rich

### 3. SqlModelConsole Struct
```rust
pub struct SqlModelConsole {
    mode: OutputMode,
    #[cfg(feature = "rich")]
    rich_console: Option<rich_rust::Console>,
    theme: Theme,
}
```

### 4. Theme System
SQLModel-specific color palette for consistent styling across all output.

## Tasks in This Phase

1. Implement OutputMode enum with detection logic (mode.rs)
2. Implement agent detection heuristics
3. Create Theme struct with SQLModel color palette
4. Implement SqlModelConsole struct
5. Add basic print methods (print, status, error)
6. Write unit tests for mode detection

## Design Principles

### Fail-Safe Default
When in doubt, use Plain mode. It's better to show plain output to a human than
to confuse an agent with ANSI codes.

### Explicit Override Always Works
`SQLMODEL_RICH=1` forces rich mode even if agent is detected. This lets developers
see rich output while testing agent workflows.

### Stream Separation
- `console.print()` → stdout (semantic data)
- `console.status()` → stderr (human feedback)

This allows agents to capture stdout for parsing while ignoring stderr.

## Dependencies (Beads)

This phase depends on Phase 1 (Foundation) being complete - the crate must exist
before we can implement its modules.

## Verification

```bash
# Test mode detection
SQLMODEL_PLAIN=1 cargo test -p sqlmodel-console --features rich mode_tests
CLAUDE_CODE=1 cargo test -p sqlmodel-console --features rich mode_tests

# Visual verification
cargo run --example mode_demo --features rich
```

SqlModelConsole struct coordinates all output
ConsoleAware trait defined for driver integration
tracing integration works for structured logging
All unit tests pass for mode detection
All unit tests pass for theme functionality

# Lazy Loading Infrastructure

## Overview
Implement lazy loading for relationships, where related objects are fetched on-demand when first accessed rather than eagerly with the parent query.

## Why This Matters
Without lazy loading, developers must:
- Always use explicit JOINs (verbose)
- Load ALL related data even when not needed
- Or write separate queries manually

Python SQLModel provides:
```python
hero = session.get(Hero, 1)  # Only fetches hero
print(hero.team.name)  # NOW fetches team (lazy)
```

## The N+1 Problem
Lazy loading CAN cause performance issues:
```python
for hero in session.exec(select(Hero)).all():
    print(hero.team.name)  # N separate queries!
```

**Our approach**: Make lazy loading OPT-IN, not default. Provide eager loading and N+1 detection.

## Rust Design Philosophy
1. **Lazy<T> wrapper type**: Explicit opt-in
2. **Connection context required**: Must have access to session/connection
3. **Deferred execution**: Query built but not run until access
4. **N+1 detection**: Optional runtime warning for query patterns

## Target API (Rust)
```rust
#[derive(Model)]
struct Hero {
    #[sqlmodel(primary_key)]
    id: Option<i64>,
    
    team_id: Option<i64>,
    
    // Eager loading (default) - loaded with JOIN or separate query
    #[sqlmodel(relationship(model = "Team"))]
    team: Related<Team>,
    
    // Lazy loading (opt-in) - loaded on first access
    #[sqlmodel(relationship(model = "Team", lazy = true))]
    team_lazy: Lazy<Team>,
}

// Usage with session:
let hero = session.get::<Hero>(1).await?;

// Eager: already loaded
let team_name = hero.team.get().name;

// Lazy: fetches now
let team_name = hero.team_lazy.load(&session).await?.name;
```

## Core Components

### 1. Lazy<T> Type
```rust
pub struct Lazy<T: Model> {
    /// The foreign key value (for lookup)
    fk_value: Option<Value>,
    /// Cached loaded value
    cached: OnceCell<Option<T>>,
    /// Marker that this needs a session to load
    _marker: PhantomData<T>,
}

impl<T: Model> Lazy<T> {
    pub async fn load(&self, session: &Session) -> Result<Option<&T>> {
        self.cached.get_or_try_init(|| async {
            match &self.fk_value {
                Some(fk) => session.get_by_fk::<T>(fk).await,
                None => Ok(None),
            }
        }).await
    }
    
    pub fn is_loaded(&self) -> bool {
        self.cached.get().is_some()
    }
}
```

### 2. LazyMany<T> Type (for collections)
```rust
pub struct LazyMany<T: Model> {
    /// Query to fetch related items
    query: Box<dyn Fn() -> SelectBuilder<T>>,
    /// Cached results
    cached: OnceCell<Vec<T>>,
}
```

### 3. Session Integration
- Session tracks which Lazy<T> have been accessed
- Can detect N+1 patterns (same query run multiple times in loop)
- Optional: batch-load detection and warning

### 4. N+1 Detection (Optional Enhancement)
```rust
session.enable_n_plus_one_detection();
// ... code that triggers N+1 ...
session.check_n_plus_one(); // Logs warning or panics in debug
```

## Success Criteria
- [ ] Lazy<T> type for single related objects
- [ ] LazyMany<T> for collections
- [ ] load() method fetches on first access
- [ ] Subsequent access uses cache
- [ ] Works with Session
- [ ] Type-safe at compile time
- [ ] Optional N+1 detection
- [ ] Can force-load (batch prefetch)

## Trade-offs & Decisions
1. **Explicit load() call**: Rust can't hide the async nature, so load() must be explicit
2. **Session required**: No way around this - need connection to fetch
3. **OnceCell for caching**: Thread-safe, init-once semantics
4. **No auto-refresh**: Load once, cached forever (within session lifecycle)

## Dependencies
- Relationship System (parent epic)
- Session/UoW (for session integration)
- Can work standalone with raw Connection if needed

## Estimated Scope
- 6-8 subtasks
- New types in sqlmodel-core
- Macro support in sqlmodel-macros
- Session integration

title: Phase 3: Error Display System
description:
# Phase 3: Error Display System

## Overview

This phase implements beautiful error display throughout sqlmodel_rust. Well-formatted
errors are one of the most impactful features because they directly help developers
debug issues faster.

## Why Error Display Matters

Current state: Errors are plain text, often missing context.

```
Error: syntax error at position 7
```

With rich error display:

```
╭─────────────────────── SQL Syntax Error ───────────────────────╮
│                                                                 │
│  Unexpected token 'SELCT' near position 7                      │
│                                                                 │
│  ┌─ Query ──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │ SELCT * FROM users WHERE id = $1                         │  │
│  │ ^^^^^                                                    │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                 │
│  💡 Hint: Did you mean 'SELECT'?                               │
│  SQLSTATE: 42601                                               │
│                                                                 │
╰─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
```

## Components to Implement

### 1. ErrorPanel Renderable
A panel specifically designed for errors with:
- Red border
- Error title based on error type
- Formatted message
- Optional SQL context with highlighting
- Optional hints
- SQLSTATE code display

### 2. Error Trait Extensions
Add methods to sqlmodel-core Error types:
- `to_panel()` → Rich panel representation
- `to_plain()` → Plain text representation
- `to_json()` → Structured JSON representation

### 3. QueryError Visualization
Special handling for QueryError which has:
- SQL statement (can be syntax highlighted)
- Error position (can be underlined)
- SQLSTATE code
- Detail and hint fields

### 4. Connection Error Display
Special handling showing:
- Host/port that failed
- Authentication details (redacted)
- Timeout information
- Retry suggestions

## Error Type Coverage

| Error Type | Rich Display |
|------------|--------------|
| Connection | Host, port, auth method, timeout |
| Query | SQL with position marker, SQLSTATE |
| Type | Expected vs actual type, value |
| Transaction | State, nested level |
| Protocol | Message type, raw bytes (redacted) |
| Pool | Pool stats, wait time |
| Schema | Table/column info, constraint |
| Config | Setting name, value, valid range |
| Io | Path, operation, errno |
| Timeout | Duration, operation |
| Cancelled | Reason, duration |

## Design Principles

### Actionable Information
Every error panel should help the user understand:
1. What went wrong
2. Where it went wrong
3. Why it went wrong (if known)
4. How to fix it (if possible)

### Privacy Aware
- Passwords are never shown
- Connection strings are redacted
- Query parameters may contain sensitive data (redact or truncate)

### Plain Mode Parity
Plain mode output must contain all the same information, just without styling.
Use indentation and ASCII art for structure.

## Tasks in This Phase

1. Create ErrorPanel renderable in sqlmodel-console
2. Implement SqlModelError trait for mode-aware display
3. Extend sqlmodel-core Error with display methods
4. Implement QueryError visualization with SQL context
5. Implement ConnectionError visualization
6. Add error examples/demos

## Dependencies (Beads)

This phase depends on Phase 2 (Core Infrastructure) being complete.
The SqlModelConsole must exist before we can add error display.

title: Implement Common Table Expressions (CTEs)
description:
## Description

Support WITH clauses for Common Table Expressions.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import select, cte

# Basic CTE
active_users = select(User).where(User.active == True).cte('active_users')

stmt = select(active_users.c.name).select_from(active_users)

# Recursive CTE
hierarchy = select(Employee).where(Employee.manager_id == None).cte('hierarchy', recursive=True)

subordinates = select(Employee).join(
    hierarchy, Employee.manager_id == hierarchy.c.id
)

hierarchy = hierarchy.union(subordinates)

stmt = select(hierarchy)
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
// Basic CTE
let active_users = select!(User)
    .filter(User::active.eq(true))
    .cte("active_users");

let query = select_from(&active_users)
    .columns(["name"]);

// Recursive CTE
let hierarchy = select!(Employee)
    .filter(Employee::manager_id.is_null())
    .cte_recursive("hierarchy");

let subordinates = select!(Employee)
    .join_cte(&hierarchy, Employee::manager_id.eq(hierarchy.col("id")));

let query = hierarchy.union(subordinates);
```

### SQL Output

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE hierarchy AS (
    SELECT * FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL
    UNION
    SELECT e.* FROM employees e 
    JOIN hierarchy h ON e.manager_id = h.id
)
SELECT * FROM hierarchy
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] cte() method creates CTE
- [ ] cte_recursive() for recursive CTEs
- [ ] CTEs can be used in FROM clause
- [ ] CTEs can be joined
- [ ] Recursive CTEs with UNION
- [ ] Multiple CTEs in single query
- [ ] All dialects supported

## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests (crates/sqlmodel-query/src/cte.rs)
- [ ] Test basic WITH clause generation
- [ ] Test CTE column aliasing
- [ ] Test multiple CTEs
- [ ] Test recursive CTE
- [ ] Test CTE reference in main query
- [ ] Test CTE with parameters

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e/query_cte.rs)
- [ ] WITH clause executes correctly
- [ ] Recursive CTE for tree traversal
- [ ] CTE for complex aggregation
- [ ] CTE referenced multiple times
- [ ] Nested CTEs (CTE referencing CTE)
- [ ] CTE performance vs subquery

### Logging
- [ ] DEBUG: CTE SQL generation
- [ ] TRACE: CTE binding resolution

title: Write comprehensive unit and integration tests for pool lock-poisoning safety

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## What

Write comprehensive unit tests and an end-to-end test script that verify the pool's new error-handling behavior after the expect()-to-Result migration.

## Where

File: crates/sqlmodel-pool/src/lib.rs (test module at bottom)
New file: crates/sqlmodel-pool/tests/poisoned_lock.rs (integration test)

## Unit Tests Required

### Error Variant Tests
1. `test_pool_poisoned_error_display` — verify the error message includes context about which operation failed
2. `test_pool_poisoned_error_debug` — verify Debug output is useful for diagnostics

### Read-Only Method Tests (after poisoning)
3. `test_config_returns_result` — verify config() returns Ok in normal case
4. `test_stats_returns_result` — verify stats() returns Ok in normal case
5. `test_at_capacity_returns_result` — verify at_capacity() returns Ok in normal case
6. `test_idle_count_returns_result` — same pattern
7. `test_total_count_returns_result` — same pattern

### Poisoned Lock Simulation Tests
8. `test_poisoned_lock_config_returns_err` — poison the mutex, verify config() returns Err (not panic)
9. `test_poisoned_lock_stats_returns_err` — same for stats()
10. `test_poisoned_lock_acquire_returns_err` — same for acquire()
11. `test_poisoned_lock_close_returns_err` — same for close()

### Drop Safety Tests
12. `test_drop_with_poisoned_lock_does_not_panic` — poison the mutex, drop a PooledConnection, verify no panic
13. `test_drop_with_poisoned_lock_logs_warning` — verify tracing output includes the error

### End-to-End Scenario Tests
14. `test_pool_survives_thread_panic` — spawn a thread that acquires a connection and panics; verify the pool still works for other threads (this is the KEY test — if it panics, the whole point of this epic fails)
15. `test_pool_graceful_degradation` — after poisoning, verify new connections can still be created (or meaningful errors are returned)

## How to Simulate Lock Poisoning

```rust
use std::sync::{Arc, Mutex};
use std::thread;

// Poison by panicking while holding the lock
let pool = create_test_pool();
let shared = pool.shared.clone(); // Need test-only accessor
let _ = thread::spawn(move || {
    let _guard = shared.inner.lock().unwrap();
    panic!("intentional test panic");
}).join();
// Now the mutex is poisoned
```

Note: This requires either:
- A `#[cfg(test)] pub(crate)` accessor for the shared state, OR
- Using the public API to trigger poisoning (harder but more realistic)

## Logging Verification

Use `tracing-test` or `tracing-subscriber` with a test layer to capture log output:
```rust
#[test]
fn test_drop_logs_on_poisoned_lock() {
    let (subscriber, handle) = tracing_test::subscriber::mock()
        .event(tracing_test::expect::event().at_level(tracing::Level::ERROR))
        .done()
        .run_with_handle();
    // ... poison lock and drop connection ...
    handle.assert_finished();
}
```

If tracing-test is not available (minimal deps policy), use a simple AtomicBool flag set in a custom tracing subscriber, or just verify no panic occurs.

## Acceptance Criteria

- At least 15 tests covering all converted methods
- Integration test that proves pool survives thread panics
- All tests pass with `cargo test -p sqlmodel-pool`
- Tests are well-documented with comments explaining what they verify
- cargo clippy clean

title: Relationship System: Complete Implementation
description:
## Overview

Implement ALL Relationship() parameters and behaviors from Python SQLModel.

## Python Relationship() Parameters

### Core Parameters
- back_populates: Optional[str] - Bidirectional relationship target
- cascade_delete: Optional[bool] - Enable cascade delete (sets cascade='all, delete-orphan')
- passive_deletes: Optional[Union[bool, Literal['all']]] - Configure passive deletes
- link_model: Optional[Any] - Secondary table for many-to-many

### SQLAlchemy Relationship Parameters
- sa_relationship: Optional[RelationshipProperty] - Full override
- sa_relationship_args: Optional[Sequence] - Extra positional args
- sa_relationship_kwargs: Optional[Mapping] - Extra keyword args

## Relationship Patterns Required

### One-to-Many
```rust
#[sqlmodel(relationship)]
children: Related<Vec<Child>>
```

### One-to-One
```rust
#[sqlmodel(relationship)]
profile: Related<Option<Profile>>
```

### Many-to-Many
```rust
#[sqlmodel(relationship, link_table = 'user_roles')]
roles: RelatedMany<Role>
```

## Missing Features

1. **Lazy Loading** - Python loads relationships on first access. Rust needs explicit equivalent that still provides convenient API.

2. **passive_deletes** - Let DB handle deletes via FK constraints instead of ORM cascade

3. **sa_relationship override** - Allow users to specify custom relationship configuration

4. **Relationship Events** - before_insert, after_insert on relationships

## Implementation Approach

For Rust, we implement lazy loading semantically via:
- Explicit load methods with clear API
- Session-tracked relationships
- Batch loading to avoid N+1
- Optional auto-load via configuration

title: Convert pool read-only methods: add lock_or_recover() with poisoning recovery

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## REFINEMENT: Consider Infallible Read-Only Accessors

### The Ergonomics Problem

Changing `config() -> PoolConfig` to `config() -> Result<PoolConfig, Error>` forces every caller to handle an error that almost never happens. This makes the common case (healthy pool) worse for every user.

### Alternative: Use unwrap_or_else with Recovery for Non-Critical Methods

For read-only methods that don't affect correctness (stats, counts), consider recovering from poisoning:

```rust
pub fn stats(&self) -> PoolStats {
    match self.shared.inner.lock() {
        Ok(inner) => inner.stats(),
        Err(poisoned) => {
            tracing::error!("Pool mutex poisoned; recovering stats from poisoned guard");
            poisoned.into_inner().stats()
        }
    }
}
```

Rationale: A poisoned mutex still contains valid data — the lock is poisoned because a HOLDER panicked, not because the data is corrupted. For read-only access, recovering via `into_inner()` is safe.

### Tier the Methods

**Tier 1 — Must return Result (mutation/acquisition):**
- `acquire()` — already returns Outcome
- `try_acquire()` — already returns Option
- `close()` — already returns Outcome
- `create_connection()` — internal, returns Result
- `evict_idle()` — internal, mutates state

**Tier 2 — Recover from poisoning (read-only, non-critical):**
- `config()` — read-only, data is always valid
- `stats()` — read-only, data is always valid
- `at_capacity()` — read-only, data is always valid
- `is_closed()` — read-only, data is always valid
- `idle_count()`, `total_count()`, `waiters_count()` — read-only

**Tier 3 — Special case (Drop):**
- `return_connection()` in Drop — must not panic, log and leak

### Updated Implementation Pattern for Tier 2

```rust
fn lock_or_recover(&self) -> std::sync::MutexGuard<'_, PoolInner<C>> {
    self.shared.inner.lock().unwrap_or_else(|poisoned| {
        tracing::error!("Pool mutex poisoned; recovering from poisoned guard");
        poisoned.into_inner()
    })
}
```

Then all Tier 2 methods use `self.lock_or_recover()` and keep their current non-Result signatures.

### Why This Is Better

- Zero API breakage for read-only methods
- Callers don't need to handle errors for stats/config
- The pool degrades gracefully instead of cascading panics
- Critical methods (acquire/close) still properly propagate errors
- The tracing::error! makes poisoning visible for debugging

### Updated Scope for bd-1uh7

This bead should implement the tiered approach:
- Add `lock_or_recover()` helper
- Use it for Tier 2 methods (NO signature change)
- Keep Tier 1 methods returning Result/Outcome (internal expect→map_err)

title: Phase 1: Foundation - Create sqlmodel-console Crate
description:
# Phase 1: Foundation - Create sqlmodel-console Crate

## Overview

This phase establishes the foundational infrastructure for the rich_rust integration by 
creating a new crate `sqlmodel-console` that will serve as the central coordination point
for all console output throughout sqlmodel_rust.

## Why a Separate Crate?

1. **Optional Dependency**: By isolating rich_rust behind a crate with feature flags, 
   users who don't need fancy output pay zero cost (no additional dependencies).

2. **Single Responsibility**: Console output concerns are separated from database logic.

3. **Consistent API**: All crates use the same SqlModelConsole interface.

4. **Testing Isolation**: Console tests don't pollute database crate tests.

## Crate Structure

```
crates/sqlmodel-console/
├── Cargo.toml              # Feature-gated rich_rust dependency
└── src/
    ├── lib.rs              # Public API, module exports, prelude
    ├── mode.rs             # OutputMode enum and detection logic
    ├── console.rs          # SqlModelConsole struct - main coordinator
    ├── theme.rs            # Color theme definitions
    ├── renderables/        # SQLModel-specific renderables
    │   └── mod.rs          # (populated in later phases)
    └── widgets/            # Progress bars, spinners
        └── mod.rs          # (populated in later phases)
```

## Key Design Decisions

### Feature Flags
```toml
[features]
default = []                  # No rich output by default
rich = ["rich_rust"]          # Basic rich output
syntax = ["rich", "rich_rust/syntax"]  # + SQL highlighting
full = ["rich", "syntax"]     # All features
```

### Conditional Compilation
All rich_rust types are behind `#[cfg(feature = "rich")]` so the crate compiles
cleanly even without the dependency. Plain mode is always available.

### Path Dependency
rich_rust is referenced as: `{ path = "../../../rich_rust", optional = true }`
This avoids crates.io publication issues and keeps the projects in sync.

## Tasks in This Phase

1. Create crate directory structure
2. Write Cargo.toml with proper feature flags
3. Create lib.rs with module declarations and prelude
4. Add crate to workspace Cargo.toml
5. Verify it builds with and without features

## Dependencies (External Crates)

- `rich_rust` (optional) - Terminal rendering
- `serde` - For theme serialization (optional)

## Verification Criteria

```bash
# Must pass:
cargo check -p sqlmodel-console
cargo check -p sqlmodel-console --features rich
cargo check -p sqlmodel-console --features full
cargo clippy -p sqlmodel-console --all-features -- -D warnings
```

## Notes for Implementer

- Follow the existing crate naming convention (sqlmodel-*)
- Use Rust 2024 edition like other crates
- Include standard #![forbid(unsafe_code)] as this is a pure Rust crate
- Add MIT/Apache-2.0 dual license header

title: Fix lossy i64-to-f64 conversion — add precision-loss detection

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## What

Add precision-loss detection to i64→f64 conversions in Value and Row.

## Where

Files:
- crates/sqlmodel-core/src/value.rs, line 436 (TryFrom<Value> for f64)
- crates/sqlmodel-core/src/row.rs (FromValue for f64)

## Details

i64 has 63 bits of precision. f64 has 53 bits of mantissa. For |i64| > 2^53 (9,007,199,254,740,992), the conversion silently rounds to the nearest representable f64.

Example: i64 value 9007199254740993 converts to f64 9007199254740992.0 — off by 1.

## Fix

```rust
Value::BigInt(v) => {
    if v.unsigned_abs() > (1u64 << 53) {
        return Err(Error::Type(TypeError {
            expected: "f64-representable integer",
            actual: format!("i64 {} exceeds f64 exact integer range (2^53)", v),
            column: None,
            rust_type: Some("f64"),
        }));
    }
    Ok(v as f64)
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- i64→f64 errors when |value| > 2^53
- Values within range convert correctly
- Tests for boundary values: 2^53, 2^53+1, -(2^53), -(2^53+1)

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## REFINEMENT: Opt-In Lossy vs Strict Conversion

### The User Experience Problem

Some users legitimately want lossy f32 conversions — for example, reading a DOUBLE column into an f32 field where they know the values are small. Making TryFrom strict by default is correct, but we should provide an escape hatch.

### Recommended Approach: Strict by Default, Lossy Helper

1. **TryFrom<Value> for f32** — STRICT (errors on precision loss). This is the default.

2. **Add a helper method on Value** — for users who accept lossy conversion:
```rust
impl Value {
    /// Convert to f32, allowing precision loss.
    /// Returns an error only for completely unrepresentable values (NaN, infinity).
    pub fn to_f32_lossy(&self) -> Result<f32, Error> { ... }

    /// Convert to f64, allowing precision loss for large integers.
    pub fn to_f64_lossy(&self) -> Result<f64, Error> { ... }
}
```

This gives users a clear choice:
- `value.try_into::<f32>()?` — strict, errors on precision loss
- `value.to_f32_lossy()?` — lenient, only errors on impossible conversions

### Scope Clarification: row.rs Must Match

The `FromValue` trait in row.rs is the OTHER path values take (database → Rust struct). It must use the same strict logic. Users who want lossy behavior in their model fields should use a wrapper type or handle it in their deserialize impl.

### Precision Loss Thresholds

For f32:
- i32 values: exact up to ±16,777,216 (2^24)
- i64 values: exact up to ±16,777,216 (same limit)
- f64 values: exact if the value is representable as f32 (check: `v as f32 as f64 == v`)

For f64:
- i64 values: exact up to ±9,007,199,254,740,992 (2^53)

### Testing Note

Test both the strict path (TryFrom) and the lossy helper (to_f32_lossy):
- Strict: verify errors at boundaries
- Lossy: verify success at same boundaries, errors only for infinity/NaN

title: Create DDL syntax highlighting for schema output
description:
## Purpose
Implement syntax highlighting for DDL (Data Definition Language) SQL statements when displaying CREATE TABLE, CREATE INDEX, and other schema-related SQL.

## Background
When displaying generated DDL or schema definitions, syntax highlighting makes the output much more readable. Keywords (CREATE, TABLE, NOT NULL) should be highlighted differently from identifiers and literals.

This uses rich_rust Syntax component with SQL language support, but we need custom handling for:
- SQL keywords in our specific dialect
- Type names (INTEGER, TEXT, VARCHAR)
- Constraints (PRIMARY KEY, REFERENCES, UNIQUE)

## Implementation Details

### File Location
crates/sqlmodel-console/src/renderables/ddl_display.rs

### Core Struct
DdlDisplay struct holds:
- sql: String - the DDL statement(s)
- dialect: SqlDialect enum (PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL)
- theme: Theme
- line_numbers: bool
- highlight_changes: Option<Vec<ChangeRegion>> - for diff highlighting

### SqlDialect Enum
PostgreSQL - includes SERIAL, BIGSERIAL, array types
SQLite - includes AUTOINCREMENT, special type handling
MySQL - includes AUTO_INCREMENT, ENGINE clause

### Rendering Strategy
1. If rich_rust syntax feature available, use Syntax component with sql language
2. Apply custom token coloring via our Theme:
   - Keywords: bold + keyword_color
   - Types: type_color
   - Strings: string_color
   - Numbers: number_color
   - Comments: comment_color (dim)
3. Optionally highlight changed regions (for migration diffs)

### API Design
DdlDisplay::new(sql)
  .dialect(SqlDialect::PostgreSQL)
  .line_numbers(true)
  .theme(theme)
  .highlight_changes(vec![ChangeRegion { start: 10, end: 20, kind: Added }])
  .render(width) / .render_plain()

### Change Highlighting (for diffs)
ChangeRegion struct: start_line, end_line, kind (Added/Removed/Modified)
- Added lines: green background
- Removed lines: red background with strikethrough
- Modified lines: yellow background

## Usage Example
let ddl = "CREATE TABLE users (
    id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
    name TEXT NOT NULL,
    email TEXT UNIQUE
);";

let display = DdlDisplay::new(ddl)
    .dialect(SqlDialect::PostgreSQL)
    .line_numbers(true);

console.print_renderable(&display);

## Plain Text Output
For agent mode, output raw SQL with optional line numbers:
  1 | CREATE TABLE users (
  2 |     id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  3 |     name TEXT NOT NULL,
  4 |     email TEXT UNIQUE
  5 | );

## Verification Steps
1. Test with each dialect (PostgreSQL, SQLite, MySQL)
2. Verify keyword highlighting
3. Test line numbers on/off
4. Test change highlighting for diffs
5. Verify plain text preserves SQL exactly
6. Test multi-statement DDL
7. Test with comments in SQL

## Dependencies
- rich_rust Syntax component (optional, behind feature flag)
- Theme from this crate
- No external SQL parser - use regex-based tokenization

All unit tests verify highlighting

title: Implement LATERAL subqueries
description:
## Description

Support LATERAL subqueries that reference outer query.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import lateral, select

subq = select(Order.id).where(
    Order.customer_id == Customer.id
).order_by(Order.date.desc()).limit(3).lateral()

stmt = select(Customer.name, subq.c.id).select_from(
    Customer.join(subq, true())
)
```

## SQL Output

```sql
SELECT c.name, recent_orders.id
FROM customers c,
LATERAL (
    SELECT o.id FROM orders o
    WHERE o.customer_id = c.id
    ORDER BY o.date DESC
    LIMIT 3
) AS recent_orders
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
let recent_orders = select!(Order)
    .filter(Order::customer_id.eq(Customer::id))
    .order_by(Order::date.desc())
    .limit(3)
    .lateral("recent_orders");

let query = select!(Customer)
    .join_lateral(&recent_orders);
```

## Dialect Support

- PostgreSQL: Full support
- MySQL 8.0+: Full support
- SQLite: Not supported (error)

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] lateral() method on Select
- [ ] join_lateral() for joining
- [ ] References outer query columns
- [ ] Correct SQL generation
- [ ] Error on unsupported dialects

## Testing Requirements

title: Implement statement caching
description:
## Description

Cache compiled SQL statements for reuse.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlalchemy import lambda_stmt

# Lazy-compiled statement
stmt = lambda_stmt(lambda: select(User).where(User.name == 'test'))

# Cached and reused on subsequent calls
result = session.exec(stmt)
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
pub struct StatementCache {
    cache: HashMap<u64, CachedStatement>,
    max_size: usize,
}

struct CachedStatement {
    sql: String,
    param_types: Vec<TypeId>,
    last_used: Instant,
}

impl StatementCache {
    pub fn get_or_compile<F: FnOnce() -> Query>(
        &mut self,
        key: u64,
        builder: F,
    ) -> &CachedStatement {
        self.cache.entry(key).or_insert_with(|| {
            let query = builder();
            CachedStatement {
                sql: query.to_sql(),
                param_types: query.param_types(),
                last_used: Instant::now(),
            }
        })
    }
}
```

### Key Generation

Use hash of query structure:
```rust
fn query_key(query: &Query) -> u64 {
    let mut hasher = DefaultHasher::new();
    query.structure_hash(&mut hasher);
    hasher.finish()
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] LRU eviction policy
- [ ] Query structure hashing
- [ ] Thread-safe access

title: Implement Identity Map
description:
## Description

Implement identity map to ensure each DB row = one Rust object in session.

## What Identity Map Does

1. **Uniqueness**: Same PK always returns same object reference
2. **Cache**: Avoid redundant queries for same object
3. **Consistency**: Changes to object visible everywhere it's used

## Python Behavior

```python
user1 = session.get(User, 1)
user2 = session.get(User, 1)
assert user1 is user2  # Same object!

user1.name = 'Changed'
print(user2.name)  # 'Changed' - it's the same object
```

## Rust Implementation

```rust
use std::any::TypeId;
use std::collections::HashMap;

pub struct IdentityMap {
    // TypeId -> (PrimaryKey -> Arc<RwLock<dyn Any>>)
    map: HashMap<TypeId, HashMap<PrimaryKeyValue, Arc<RwLock<Box<dyn Any>>>>>,
}

impl IdentityMap {
    pub fn get<M: Model + 'static>(&self, pk: &PrimaryKeyValue) -> Option<Arc<RwLock<M>>> {
        self.map
            .get(&TypeId::of::<M>())?
            .get(pk)?
            .clone()
            .downcast()
            .ok()
    }
    
    pub fn insert<M: Model + 'static>(&mut self, model: M) -> Arc<RwLock<M>> {
        let pk = model.primary_key_value();
        let arc = Arc::new(RwLock::new(model));
        self.map
            .entry(TypeId::of::<M>())
            .or_default()
            .insert(pk, arc.clone());
        arc
    }
}
```

## Challenges in Rust

1. **Ownership**: Can't have multiple owners without Arc
2. **Mutability**: Need interior mutability (RwLock)
3. **Type erasure**: Need Any + downcast

## Alternative: Weak references

Use Weak<> to allow objects to be dropped when not in use:
```rust
map: HashMap<TypeId, HashMap<PrimaryKeyValue, Weak<RwLock<dyn Any>>>>
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Same PK returns same object
- [ ] Objects are reference-counted
- [ ] Modifications visible to all references
- [ ] Clear on session close
- [ ] Works with composite PKs

## Testing Requirements

### Unit Tests (crates/sqlmodel-core/src/session/identity_map.rs)
- [ ] Test basic get/set operations
- [ ] Test same PK returns same object reference
- [ ] Test different objects with same data are identity-equal
- [ ] Test clear() removes all entries
- [ ] Test contains() for existing and non-existing keys
- [ ] Test memory leak prevention (weak references if applicable)

### E2E Tests (tests/e2e/session_identity_map.rs)
- [ ] Query same row twice → same Rust object
- [ ] Modify via one reference → visible via other
- [ ] Session.add() with existing PK → proper conflict handling
- [ ] Concurrent access from multiple tasks
- [ ] Cross-session isolation (different sessions, different maps)

### Logging
- [ ] TRACE: Identity map hits/misses
- [ ] DEBUG: Object registration/eviction
- [ ] INFO: Map statistics on session close

title: Implement lazy loading for relationships
description:
## Description

Implement lazy loading semantics for relationships in Rust.

## Python Behavior

```python
class Team(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: int
    heroes: List['Hero'] = Relationship(back_populates='team')

# Lazy loading - heroes loaded on first access
team = session.get(Team, 1)
print(team.heroes)  # SQL query executed HERE
```

## Rust Approach

Since Rust doesn't have implicit property access hooks, we use explicit loading:

### Option 1: LazyRelated<T> wrapper
```rust
#[derive(Model)]
struct Team {
    id: i32,
    
    #[sqlmodel(relationship, lazy)]
    heroes: LazyRelated<Vec<Hero>>,
}

impl Team {
    async fn heroes(&self, cx: &Cx, session: &Session) -> Outcome<&[Hero], Error> {
        self.heroes.load(cx, session).await
    }
}
```

### Option 2: Session method
```rust
let heroes = session.load_related(cx, &team, Team::heroes).await?;
```

### Option 3: Auto-load configuration
```rust
#[sqlmodel(relationship, load = "auto")]
heroes: Related<Vec<Hero>>,
```

## Requirements

1. Track which relationships are loaded
2. Load on explicit request
3. Support batch loading to avoid N+1
4. Cache loaded relationships
5. Clear cache on refresh

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] LazyRelated<T> type implemented
- [ ] Load method fetches from database

- [ ] Works with Session context

title: Implement Session.refresh()
description:
## Description

Immediately reload object from database.

## Python Behavior

```python
# Reload all attributes
session.refresh(user)

# Reload specific attributes
session.refresh(user, ['name', 'email'])

# With options (eager load relationships)
session.refresh(user, with_for_update=True)
```

Unlike expire(), refresh() immediately queries the DB.

## Rust Implementation

```rust
impl Session {
    pub async fn refresh<M: Model>(
        &mut self,
        cx: &Cx,
        model: &mut M,
        attributes: Option<&[&str]>,
    ) -> Outcome<(), Error> {
        let pk = model.primary_key_value();
        
        // Query database
        let fresh: M = select!(M)
            .filter(M::primary_key().eq(pk))
            .one(cx, &self.conn)
            .await?;
        
        // Update model
        match attributes {
            Some(attrs) => model.copy_attributes_from(&fresh, attrs),
            None => *model = fresh,
        }
        
        // Update identity map
        self.identity_map.update(model);
        
        Ok(())
    }
}
```

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] Immediately queries database
- [ ] Updates model with fresh values
- [ ] Can refresh specific attributes only
- [ ] Updates identity map
- [ ] Errors if object not in DB (was deleted)

## Testing Requirements

## What

Add integration tests that verify SQL identifier quoting works end-to-end for pathological table/column names.

## Where

New test module in crates/sqlmodel-schema/src/create.rs or a dedicated test file.

## Test Cases

1. Table name with embedded double-quote: `user"table` → `"user""table"`
2. Table name that is a SQL keyword: `select` → `"select"`
3. Column name with spaces: `first name` → `"first name"`
4. Empty table name → error (not empty quotes)
5. Table name with null byte → error or stripped
6. Unicode table name: `用户` → `"用户"`
7. DROP TABLE with quoted name: verify the SQL is syntactically correct
8. CREATE TABLE with quoted column names
9. INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE with quoted identifiers
10. MySQL backtick quoting equivalents

## Acceptance Criteria

- Tests run in cargo test --all
- No new dependencies added

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## What

Write comprehensive unit tests and integration tests verifying SQL identifier quoting works correctly across all crates — the shared utility, the schema DDL, the session flush DML, and the migration runner.

## Where

Files:
- crates/sqlmodel-core/src/types.rs or identifiers.rs — unit tests for quote_ident()

## Unit Tests for quote_ident() Utility

### ANSI Double-Quote Style
1. `test_quote_ident_simple` — `quote_ident("users")` → `"\"users\""`
2. `test_quote_ident_empty` — `quote_ident("")` → `"\"\""` (valid SQL, means empty-string identifier)
3. `test_quote_ident_embedded_double_quote` — `quote_ident("user\"name")` → `"\"user\"\"name\""`
4. `test_quote_ident_multiple_quotes` — `quote_ident("a\"b\"c")` → `"\"a\"\"b\"\"c\""`
5. `test_quote_ident_sql_keyword` — `quote_ident("select")` → `"\"select\""` (safe from keyword collision)
6. `test_quote_ident_spaces` — `quote_ident("first name")` → `"\"first name\""`
7. `test_quote_ident_unicode` — `quote_ident("用户")` → `"\"用户\""`
8. `test_quote_ident_semicolon` — `quote_ident("a;b")` → `"\"a;b\""` (semicolons inside quotes are safe)
9. `test_quote_ident_newline` — `quote_ident("a\nb")` → `"\"a\nb\""` (newlines inside quotes are safe)
10. `test_quote_ident_null_byte` — `quote_ident("a\0b")` → should either strip the null or error (discuss)
11. `test_quote_ident_backslash` — `quote_ident("a\\b")` → `"\"a\\b\""` (backslash is literal in ANSI SQL)
12. `test_quote_ident_only_quotes` — `quote_ident("\"\"")` → `"\"\"\"\"\"\"\""`

### MySQL Backtick Style
13. `test_quote_ident_mysql_simple` — `quote_ident_mysql("users")` → `` "`users`" ``

21. `test_sanitize_empty_input` — `sanitize_identifier("")` → `""` (caller should handle)

title: Implement passive_deletes for relationships
description:
## Description

Support passive_deletes to let database handle cascade deletes.

## Python Behavior

```python
class Parent(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: int
    children: List['Child'] = Relationship(
        back_populates='parent',
        passive_deletes=True  # Let DB handle deletes via FK ON DELETE
    )
    
    # With 'all', don't even warn about orphans
    children2: List['Child'] = Relationship(passive_deletes='all')
```

When passive_deletes=True:
- SQLAlchemy doesn't emit DELETE for children
- Relies on DB's ON DELETE CASCADE
- More efficient for large collections

## Rust Implementation

```rust
#[derive(Model)]
struct Parent {
    id: i32,
    
    #[sqlmodel(relationship, passive_deletes)]
    children: Related<Vec<Child>>,
    
    #[sqlmodel(relationship, passive_deletes = "all")]
    children2: Related<Vec<Child>>,
}
```

## Behavior

- passive_deletes=false (default): ORM deletes related objects
- passive_deletes=true: ORM relies on DB cascade
- passive_deletes='all': Don't even track orphans

title: Implement dynamic model creation
description:
## Description

Create models dynamically at runtime.

## Python Behavior

```python
from sqlmodel import SQLModel, Field
from typing import Optional

def create_model(name: str, fields: dict):
    return type(name, (SQLModel,), {
        '__annotations__': fields,
        '__tablename__': name.lower(),
    })

DynamicUser = create_model('DynamicUser', {
    'id': Optional[int],
    'name': str,
})
```

## Rust Approach

Rust's static typing makes true dynamic models impossible, but we can:

### Option 1: Generic Dynamic Model
```rust
pub struct DynamicModel {
    table_name: String,
    columns: HashMap<String, ColumnDef>,
    values: HashMap<String, Value>,
}

impl DynamicModel {
    pub fn new(table_name: &str) -> Self { ... }
    pub fn add_column(&mut self, name: &str, def: ColumnDef) { ... }
    pub fn set(&mut self, name: &str, value: Value) { ... }
    pub fn get(&self, name: &str) -> Option<&Value> { ... }
}
```

### Option 2: Schema from database
```rust
let schema = introspect_table(cx, conn, "users").await?;
let dynamic = DynamicModel::from_schema(schema);
```

## Use Cases

- Database introspection tools
- Generic admin interfaces
- Schema migration tools

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] DynamicModel type
- [ ] Runtime column definition
- [ ] Query execution with dynamic models
- [ ] Serialization to/from JSON

title: Implement IndeterminateSpinner for unknown-length operations
description:
## Purpose
Create a spinner renderable for operations where we do not know the total count or duration, showing activity with elapsed time.

## Background
Many database operations have unknown duration:
- Establishing connections
- Running complex queries
- Waiting for locks
- Initial data discovery

Users need feedback that something is happening, even without a completion percentage.

## Implementation Details

### File Location
crates/sqlmodel-console/src/renderables/spinner.rs

### Core Struct
IndeterminateSpinner holds:
- message: String
- started_at: Instant
- style: SpinnerStyle enum
- theme: Theme

### SpinnerStyle Enum
- Dots: ... (three dots cycling)
- Braille: Unicode braille pattern animation
- Line: -/|\ rotating
- Arrow: arrow rotating
- Simple: asterisk blinking

### Frame Generation
Each style defines frames array and interval_ms.
Example Dots: [".", "..", "...", ".."] at 250ms intervals

### Rendering (Rich Mode)
[...] Connecting to database (2.3s)
^---- spinner animation
     ^---- message
                           ^---- elapsed time

### Plain Text (Agent Mode)
[...] Connecting to database (2.3s)
(Static output, no animation - agents see single line)

## API Design
IndeterminateSpinner::new(message)
  .style(SpinnerStyle::Dots)
  .theme(theme)
  .render(width) / .render_plain()

### Convert to Progress
When length becomes known, convert spinner to progress:
let progress = spinner.into_progress(total);

### Live Update Pattern
let spinner = IndeterminateSpinner::new("Connecting");
console.start_spinner(&spinner);
// ... do work
console.stop_spinner(&spinner);

## Verification Steps
1. Test each spinner style
2. Verify elapsed time formatting (s, m:ss)
3. Test conversion to progress bar
4. Verify plain text output
5. Test with long messages (truncation)
6. Verify animation timing

## Dependencies
- Theme from this crate
- std::time::Instant for timing

Spinner has multiple style options
Spinner respects terminal width
Plain mode outputs dots or status text

title: Fix lossy f32 conversions — add precision-loss detection
close_reason: Added precision loss detection to TryFrom<Value> for f32/f64 and FromValue for f32/f64, plus to_f32_lossy()/to_f64_lossy() helpers

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## REFINEMENT: Opt-In Lossy vs Strict Conversion

### The User Experience Problem

Some users legitimately want lossy f32 conversions — for example, reading a DOUBLE column into an f32 field where they know the values are small. Making TryFrom strict by default is correct, but we should provide an escape hatch.

### Recommended Approach: Strict by Default, Lossy Helper

1. **TryFrom<Value> for f32** — STRICT (errors on precision loss). This is the default.

2. **Add a helper method on Value** — for users who accept lossy conversion:
```rust
impl Value {
    /// Convert to f32, allowing precision loss.
    /// Returns an error only for completely unrepresentable values (NaN, infinity).
    pub fn to_f32_lossy(&self) -> Result<f32, Error> { ... }

    /// Convert to f64, allowing precision loss for large integers.
    pub fn to_f64_lossy(&self) -> Result<f64, Error> { ... }
}
```

This gives users a clear choice:
- `value.try_into::<f32>()?` — strict, errors on precision loss
- `value.to_f32_lossy()?` — lenient, only errors on impossible conversions

### Scope Clarification: row.rs Must Match

The `FromValue` trait in row.rs is the OTHER path values take (database → Rust struct). It must use the same strict logic. Users who want lossy behavior in their model fields should use a wrapper type or handle it in their deserialize impl.

### Precision Loss Thresholds

For f32:
- i32 values: exact up to ±16,777,216 (2^24)
- i64 values: exact up to ±16,777,216 (same limit)
- f64 values: exact if the value is representable as f32 (check: `v as f32 as f64 == v`)

For f64:
- i64 values: exact up to ±9,007,199,254,740,992 (2^53)

### Testing Note

Test both the strict path (TryFrom) and the lossy helper (to_f32_lossy):
- Strict: verify errors at boundaries
- Lossy: verify success at same boundaries, errors only for infinity/NaN

comments.author: Dicklesworthstone
comments.text:
## SCOPE: This task MUST update BOTH files:
1. crates/sqlmodel-core/src/value.rs (TryFrom<Value> for f32) 
2. crates/sqlmodel-core/src/row.rs (FromValue for f32)
Both paths must have identical precision checks. Also add to_f32_lossy() and to_f64_lossy() helpers on Value for users who want lenient conversions.

title: EPIC: Session & Unit of Work Pattern
description:
# Session & Unit of Work Pattern

## Overview
Implement the Session abstraction that provides:
1. **Unit of Work**: Track all changes to objects, batch them, commit atomically
2. **Identity Map**: Cache objects by primary key, ensure same row = same object
3. **Change Tracking**: Know which objects are new/modified/deleted
4. **Lifecycle Management**: add(), delete(), flush(), commit(), rollback()

## Why This Matters
Without Session/UoW, users must:
- Manually track which objects need INSERT vs UPDATE
- Manually manage transactions for every operation
- Risk having two different Rust objects for the same database row
- Write explicit INSERT/UPDATE for every save operation

Python SQLModel provides:
```python
with Session(engine) as session:
    hero = Hero(name="Spider-Man")
    session.add(hero)  # Tracks as "new"
    
    hero.age = 26  # Automatically tracked as "dirty"
    
    session.commit()  # Batches: INSERT hero, then UPDATE hero
```

## Rust Design Philosophy
Rust's ownership model actually HELPS here:
1. **Session owns tracked objects** (or holds references)
2. **Interior mutability** for change tracking (RefCell or similar)
3. **Explicit flush points** (no implicit autoflush on query)
4. **Compile-time safety** for lifecycle violations

## Target API (Rust)
```rust
let session = Session::new(pool.acquire().await?);

// Add new object
let mut hero = Hero::new("Spider-Man");
session.add(&mut hero);

// Modify tracked object
hero.age = Some(26);  // Session detects this via marker

// Query (doesn't auto-flush by default)
let heroes = session.query::<Hero>()
    .filter(Expr::col("age").gt(18))
    .all()
    .await?;

// Explicit flush batches all pending changes
session.flush().await?;

// Commit the transaction
session.commit().await?;
```

## Core Components

### 1. Session Struct
- Holds connection (or pool reference)
- Maintains identity map
- Tracks pending operations (new, dirty, deleted)
- Manages transaction state

### 2. Identity Map
- HashMap<(TypeId, PrimaryKey), Tracked<T>>
- Ensures get(Hero, 1) returns same object
- Weak references to allow cleanup

### 3. Change Tracking
- "Clean" state snapshot on load/add
- Compare current vs clean to detect changes
- Track which fields changed (for partial UPDATE)

### 4. Flush Strategy
- Order operations: DELETE first (FK safety), then INSERT, then UPDATE
- Topological sort for FK dependencies
- Batch similar operations

## Success Criteria
- [ ] session.add(obj) tracks new objects
- [ ] session.delete(obj) marks for deletion
- [ ] Dirty detection works for field changes
- [ ] session.flush() batches operations correctly
- [ ] session.commit() commits transaction
- [ ] session.rollback() discards changes
- [ ] Identity map prevents duplicate objects
- [ ] session.get::<T>(pk) uses identity map
- [ ] Works with async/await via asupersync

## Architecture Decisions
1. **Explicit flush**: No autoflush on query (predictable performance)
2. **Session borrows objects**: Use RefCell<T> for interior mutability
3. **Tracked<T> wrapper**: Holds original state for diff
4. **No global session**: Must pass session explicitly (Rust idiom)

## Dependencies
- Connection/Pool (done)
- Transaction support (done)
- Model trait with PK access (done)

## Estimated Scope
- 10-15 subtasks
- New crate: sqlmodel-session (or in sqlmodel-core)
- Significant macro work for change tracking
close_reason: done
